question: What is the primary purpose of Alabama's Real Estate Consumer's Agency and Disclosure Act (RECAD)?
choice_a: To set the maximum commission a broker may charge on a residential sale
choice_b: To establish which types of agency relationships a real estate licensee may have with buyers and sellers and require disclosure of those relationships to consumers
choice_c: To require every buyer to hire a licensed attorney to review the purchase contract
choice_d: To create the state's residential property condition disclosure form used in every sale
explanation: RECAD (its official short title, per Ala. Code Sec. 34-27-80, is the 'Real Estate Consumer's Agency and Disclosure Act') is Article 4 of Chapter 27, Title 34. Section 34-27-82 requires a licensee to act as a single agent, dual agent, or transaction facilitator, and to disclose that relationship (and the services available) to the consumer before providing brokerage services. RECAD does not regulate commission amounts, mandate attorney review, or create a separate property condition disclosure form.
source_note: Ala. Code Sec. 34-27-80 through 34-27-88 (Title 34, Ch. 27, Art. 4); purpose/disclosure mechanics chiefly in Sec. 34-27-82(a)-(c). Verified against the full live statutory text of Article 4 published by the Alabama Real Estate Commission (arec.alabama.gov, License Law section), 2026-09-02.

question: Under RECAD, what is a 'designated single agent'?
choice_a: The broker of record who personally supervises every transaction in the firm
choice_b: A licensee hired directly by the Alabama Real Estate Commission to investigate consumer complaints
choice_c: When two or more licensees under the same qualifying broker have separate agency agreements with different parties to the same transaction, a designated single agent is one of those licensees whom the qualifying broker designates to represent only that licensee's own client -- this arrangement is not treated as dual agency
choice_d: Any licensee who has completed post-licensing education
explanation: Section 34-27-82(g) provides that when two or more licensees under the same qualifying broker are each in separate agency agreements with a different party to the same transaction, the qualifying broker may designate those licensees as single agents as to each licensee's own client. A designated single agent is expressly not a dual agent, and no licensee involved is assumed to have knowledge held by another licensee's own client. RECAD's definitions section (Sec. 34-27-81) does not separately define a standalone term 'designated agent' -- the mechanism appears as 'designated single agent' within Sec. 34-27-82(g) itself.
source_note: Ala. Code Sec. 34-27-82(g). Verified against the live statutory text (arec.alabama.gov License Law section), 2026-09-02.

question: Under RECAD, what must occur before a licensee acts as a dual agent representing both the buyer and the seller in the same transaction?
choice_a: Only the seller's consent is required, since the seller pays the commission
choice_b: The Alabama Real Estate Commission must approve the transaction in advance
choice_c: Dual agency is prohibited outright in Alabama under all circumstances
choice_d: All clients involved must give their prior written, informed consent to the dual agency arrangement
explanation: Section 34-27-81(8) defines dual agency as an agency relationship in which the licensee, with the informed written consent of all parties, represents both the seller and the buyer once all parties have signed the consent agreement. Section 34-27-85(c) confirms that a licensee may provide brokerage services as a dual agent only with the prior written, informed consent of all clients of the licensee in the transaction.
source_note: Ala. Code Sec. 34-27-81(8) (definition) and Sec. 34-27-85(c) (consent requirement). Verified against the live statutory text, 2026-09-02.

question: Under RECAD, in addition to the baseline obligations every licensee owes to all parties in a transaction (Sec. 34-27-84), what additional duties does Sec. 34-27-85 impose specifically on a licensee representing a 'client'?
choice_a: To loyally place the client's interests ahead of any other party's (unless doing so would violate duties owed to other parties under Sec. 34-27-84), to disclose to the client all material information known to the licensee, and to fulfill the client's lawful instructions under the agency agreement
choice_b: Only a duty of basic honesty and fair dealing, identical to what every party is already owed
choice_c: No duties beyond delivering a copy of the purchase contract
choice_d: A duty to represent the opposing party equally in every negotiation
explanation: Section 34-27-85(a) lists three duties owed only to a client, layered on top of the universal obligations in Sec. 34-27-84: (1) loyally representing the client's best interests ahead of any other party's, unless that conflicts with duties owed to others under Sec. 34-27-84; (2) disclosing to the client all material information known to the licensee and not reasonably discoverable by the client; and (3) fulfilling the agency agreement and the client's lawful instructions. Reasonable skill and care, confidentiality, and accounting for funds/property are NOT client-exclusive under current Alabama law -- Sec. 34-27-84 requires those of a licensee toward every party, including customers.
source_note: Ala. Code Sec. 34-27-85(a), read together with Sec. 34-27-84. Verified against the live statutory text, 2026-09-02.

question: Under RECAD, what duties does Sec. 34-27-84 require a licensee to provide to every party in a real estate transaction, including a 'customer' the licensee does not represent as agent?
choice_a: The exact same loyalty and material-fact-disclosure duties owed to a client
choice_b: To act honestly and in good faith, to exercise reasonable skill and care, to keep certain information confidential, to account for that party's funds or property in the licensee's possession, to present written offers in a timely and truthful manner, and to disclose the licensee's own personal interest in the transaction
choice_c: No duties whatsoever, since the licensee has no agency relationship with that party
choice_d: A duty to negotiate the lowest possible price on the customer's behalf
explanation: Section 34-27-84(a) lists six obligations a licensee owes to ALL parties in a transaction, not just clients: honesty and good faith, reasonable skill and care, confidentiality (of information given in confidence, or that a reasonable person would want kept confidential, subject to listed exceptions), accounting for property received, timely and truthful presentation of written offers, and written disclosure of the licensee's own personal interest. A customer does not additionally receive the client-only duties of loyalty or affirmative disclosure of material facts under Sec. 34-27-85, but confidentiality and reasonable skill/care ARE owed to customers -- contrary to a common misconception that only clients get those protections.
source_note: Ala. Code Sec. 34-27-84(a). Verified against the live statutory text, 2026-09-02.

question: Under RECAD, can an agency relationship with a consumer be created simply because a licensee will be compensated through that consumer's side of the transaction (for example, receiving part of a commission through a cooperating brokerage split), without anything more?
choice_a: Yes, whoever ultimately pays the licensee is automatically that licensee's client
choice_b: Yes, but only in commercial transactions, not residential ones
choice_c: No -- Sec. 34-27-82(b) provides that an agency relationship shall not be assumed, implied, or created except by a written bilateral agency agreement signed by the licensee and the consumer, so a compensation arrangement alone does not create or negate agency
choice_d: RECAD does not address how or when an agency relationship is formed
explanation: Section 34-27-82(b) states that a licensee is considered a transaction facilitator, not an agent, until a broker enters into a specific written agreement establishing an agency relationship, and that an agency relationship 'shall not be assumed, implied, or created' without a signed written bilateral agency agreement. That written-agreement requirement is what determines agency status -- not the source or path of the licensee's compensation.
source_note: Ala. Code Sec. 34-27-82(b). Verified against the live statutory text, 2026-09-02.

question: Which relationships does RECAD currently recognize for how a licensee may serve a party in a real estate transaction?
choice_a: Only single agency; all other arrangements are illegal in Alabama
choice_b: Only dual agency, which is mandatory in every transaction
choice_c: Subagency and franchise agency, which remain the exclusive relationship types under current Alabama law
choice_d: Single agency (as a buyer's agent or seller's agent) and dual agency (with all clients' prior written, informed consent), or otherwise the licensee is a transaction facilitator -- with a qualifying broker also able to designate two different in-house licensees as separate single agents, one per party, in the same deal
explanation: Section 34-27-82(a) states that a licensee may act as a single agent, dual agent, or transaction facilitator. Section 34-27-81 defines 'single agent' (buyer's agent or seller's agent) and 'dual agency,' and Sec. 34-27-82(g) allows a qualifying broker to designate two different licensees within the same firm as separate single agents for the two sides of one in-house transaction. RECAD's current definitions (as amended, most recently substantively by Act 2008-141) do NOT define or recognize 'subagency' as a relationship type -- that concept from older, generic agency-law frameworks was superseded when the transaction-facilitator category was added to Alabama law by Act 98-618.
source_note: Ala. Code Sec. 34-27-82(a) and (g); definitions in Sec. 34-27-81. Verified against the live statutory text, 2026-09-02.

question: Under RECAD, what is the default status of a licensee's relationship with a consumer at initial contact, before any written agency agreement is signed?
choice_a: The licensee is a transaction facilitator, not an agent of that consumer, and stays in that role unless and until a broker enters into a written agreement establishing an agency relationship
choice_b: The licensee automatically becomes a dual agent representing both sides
choice_c: The licensee automatically becomes a single agent for whichever party made contact first
choice_d: No relationship exists and the licensee owes no duties of any kind until a contract is signed
explanation: Section 34-27-82(b) provides that at initial contact, and until a broker enters a specific written agreement establishing an agency relationship, the licensee is considered a transaction facilitator, not an agent, of that consumer. Even as a transaction facilitator the licensee still owes the baseline duties in Sec. 34-27-84 to that consumer; the licensee simply is not yet anyone's fiduciary agent.
source_note: Ala. Code Sec. 34-27-82(b). Verified against the live statutory text, 2026-09-02.

question: Under RECAD, every offer to purchase must prominently display a representation disclosure clause. What must that clause state about the listing licensee and the selling licensee?
choice_a: The exact dollar amount of commission each licensee will receive from the transaction
choice_b: Whether each one is an agent of the buyer, a dual agent, or is instead assisting the seller or buyer as a transaction facilitator, completed and initialed as part of the offer
choice_c: Each licensee's total continuing education hours completed for the current renewal cycle
choice_d: The buyer's credit score and loan pre-approval amount
explanation: Section 34-27-82(i) requires every offer to purchase to prominently display a representation disclosure clause, completed and initialed, in which the listing licensee and the selling licensee each check whether they are an agent of the buyer, a dual agent, or assisting the seller/buyer as a transaction facilitator.
source_note: Ala. Code Sec. 34-27-82(i). Verified against the live statutory text, 2026-09-02.

question: Under RECAD, if a licensee passes along false information about a property that was originally given to the licensee by that licensee's own client, is the licensee liable to the other party for that misrepresentation?
choice_a: Yes, licensees are strictly liable for relaying any false information regardless of their own knowledge
choice_b: Only if the transaction ultimately fails to close
choice_c: Not unless the licensee knew or should have known that the information was false
choice_d: RECAD does not address misrepresentation liability; that is left entirely to common-law fraud principles
explanation: Section 34-27-86(b) provides that a licensee is not liable for providing false information to a party if that information was supplied to the licensee by the licensee's own client, by a customer, or by another licensee -- unless the licensee knew or should have known the information was false. Section 34-27-86(a) similarly shields a client from liability for a licensee's own misrepresentation unless the client knew or should have known of it.
source_note: Ala. Code Sec. 34-27-86(a)-(b). Verified against the live statutory text, 2026-09-02.
